articleTitle: Application of artificial intelligence techniques to decentralised decision making in C/sup 3/-MIS
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The paper is a first step in a research effort to develop the required theoretical and algorithmic tools for the systematic analysis and design of C/sup 3/-MIS systems. It considers the use of a stochastic learning automata approach for both the adaptive control and modelling of decentralised decision making in C/sup 3/-MIS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Architectures for C/sup 2/ knowledge-based systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Covers architectural issues of knowledge representation, with particular emphasis on the attainment of adequate real-time performance. Performance measurements of blackboard and production systems are compared, and exploratory research on the use of parallel and connectionist architectures is reported.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The battlefield sensor simulator
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The battlefield sensor simulator (BSS) is a facility for very high resolution simulation of the performance of sensors on the battlefield and has been particularly conceived to evaluate the sensor fusion and communication aspects of that performance. The facility, as described, is a large, transputer-based processing system designed to handle the movements of the objects on the battlefield, the sensors observing them and the processes necessary to determine which sensors see which targets and with what signal-to-noise ratio. The paper addresses the design approach, the tools used in the design process and the current stage of the implementation of that design. The system in its present form has over 100 processors, 250 MBytes of RAM, and several GBytes of both tape and disc memory. It has a nominal processing power of about 1000 transputer RISC MIPS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rapid prototyping of MMI as applied to C3I system architectures
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The paper brings together ideas of a layered model for describing MMI together with a conceptual framework for C3I system design and MMI prototyping. It shows how CISAT can be used as a practical tool to support prototyping during C3I system design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Developing an integrated approach to the management of dynamic data (water industry)
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Describes a project undertaken by Welsh Water to develop its management information system. The basic information is derived from telemetry data. The project described is exemplary in its orchestration, from initial concept through to completion and forms a useful model from which, to date, a great deal has been learned.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: C3MIS in the advanced air traffic control system (AAS)
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The US is about to begin the upgrade of its total air traffic control system. The Advanced Automation Program replaces both the en-route and terminal approach control air traffic control computer systems over the next decade. The AAS will provide the computers, software, and controller work stations for integrated en-route and terminal radar. The AAS will also include a tower control computer complex for use by the controllers in the towers. This new system will replace the en-route and terminal computers, flight strip printers, display equipment and the backup radar display system. The author discusses the system architecture, the user interface, the control center and software engineering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of communications and information systems architectures: a methodology and toolset
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: A four stage methodology and supporting computer based tools are described. These have been specifically developed to assist in defining a goal architecture for future RN CIS. The key products of the methodology are (i) the information exchange requirements (IERs) needed to support operations, and (ii) the definition of a CIS architecture that will meet that requirement. The IER is developed with the assistance of the C2IR system, whilst the enabling architecture is identified from candidate architectures with the assistance of the ISAT.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Command center analyses supporting requirements specification
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The modular command and control evaluation structure (MCES), imposes a consistent way of looking at the elements of a problem. Thus, the similarities (and the differences) between a set of different approaches to the same class of problems are highlighted. The approach is to match concepts. The question should be 'How can we maximize our analysis by leveraging upon the insights provided by other analyses?' This is achieved through the development of a set of generic principles. These, in turn, provide a strawman for the solution of new problems. In this way, requirements specifications for command center (CC) architectures are supported. Clearly, this approach implies the building of a database of similar studies, both those analyzed with the same and those using differing methodologies. Additionally, the building of a community of analysts who share common concerns is implied. This process is more efficient using a standard methodology across problems. To this end, the MCES has been proposed for use in evaluating C2 systems and architectures (S/A) across services and mission areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Operational use of knowledge-based military C/sup 2/ systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Presents a customer's view of knowledge-based military C/sup 2/ systems. The viewpoint presented is that of the Captain, Naval Operational Command Systems (CNOCS), the authority responsible for formulating the requirement for all naval C/sup 2/ systems. Issues of specification, procurement, management and ownership of a tactical knowledge base are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Allegiance assessment using explanation-based reasoning
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Discusses the particular problem of allegiance assessment and the system attributes required to undertake it, summarises some of the limitations in this context of 'traditional' methods of handling uncertainty, describes the principles of explanation-based reasoning, and shows, with examples from an illustrative Ada implementation, how it can be used to carry out allegiance assessment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: TESS: a mobility expert system
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Describes TESS, a mobility expert system that employs knowledge based techniques to reason about the factors that influence unit movement. As a result, it can produce accurate and timely estimates of unit travel times, and qualitative predictions about unit behaviour. It can be used as both a component of a data fusion system, or as a stand-alone decision support system. TESS is currently being implemented using ESB, a sophisticated knowledge based system construction tool. Following a review of the problem area, the paper presents a general overview of the TESS architecture, and a gives functional outline of each major component. It then discusses the TESS route evaluation mechanism, paying particular attention to the role of artificial intelligence techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Managing military mobile communications networks
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Discusses the evolution of computer assisted management of communications networks which contain mobile nodes. The author reviews: the basic facilities provided by a typical management system; the history of the evolution through the BRUIN Management Information System via the Ptarmigan System Control Computer to the MRS Network Management Processor; the current state of management products; the current relationship with civilian systems; the near and medium term future and the influence of fourth generation languages and artificial intelligence.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Raising standards in command control and communications
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Examines the growing developments of models for C3, and their role in achieving greater interoperability, and more controlled system procurement. The author reviews OSI and other layered models for communication systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Data integration and MIS in the water industry
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The typical UK water authority owns and operates a wide variety of computerised information systems. Each of these typically handles data that may be related to data on other systems, but generally the interfaces between the systems are limited to manual data interchange or the input of subjectively derived data synopses. Inefficient use of data is costly and can be potentially disastrous. As a result, trends in information technology in the industry are towards systems which integrate data and can provide high-level management decision support information. The article outlines some of the management problems facing the UK water industry, and describes an operational information management system, designed to satisfy the above criteria, which is currently undergoing prototype evaluation in a UK water authority.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience of implementation from a formal specification
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The paper is concerned with the practical realities of using formal specifications in the implementation of complex systems, such as C3MIS, with the objective of ensuring safety or security. It first considers the question of what is meant by a formal specification, why formal specifications are increasingly being demanded in defence systems and why there appears to be a problem with achieving the objectives set for their use. The problems are discussed in more detail, with reference to a particular implementation project, although details have been simplified and modified for pedagogical and security reasons. Finally, the paper discusses what, in the author's view, is and is not practicable to expect from formal specifications in the near to medium term.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Command system requirements definition
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: A previous paper, at last years conference, by Holman, Young, and Dovrington described a method which had been developed to define the requirements for surface naval command systems. The method has now been applied to a particular system. A number of problems have been identified. This paper discusses some of these problems and indicates how some of them may be overcome. An important feature of any method is its tool support. This paper also discusses the current tools in terms of their advantages and disadvantages, and indicates where suitable tools can be used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Data fusion technology forecast for C/sup 3/MIS
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Surveys three areas of rapid technology advancement that have the potential for significant improvements in data fusion/C/sup 3/MIS systems over the next decade: the area of tracker-correlators to achieve consistent tracking performance over a wide range of target and background conditions. Symbolic computational methods and artificial intelligence techniques which provide perceptual interpretation, intelligent reasoning, and learning capabilities for fusion. Parallel and high-connected processor/memory architectures which enhance the speed, fault-tolerance and associative capabilities of data fusion system implementations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interoperability-how do we know when we have achieved it? (Military systems)
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Whenever disparate systems are required to exchange information there will be a need for a test programme to evaluate the extent of interoperability that can be achieved. The increasing complexity of C3MIS, the variety of different systems that are required to exchange information, and the incompatibilities that can occur due to differences in implementation and timescales, create significant problems for the coordinating agencies involved. The article describes various issues concerned with the analysis, expression and measurement of interoperability and puts forward a metric based upon achievement of interoperability requirements. It uses as its basis the concept of a generalised defence system comprising a number of separate platforms. The principles, however, are applicable to any complex C3MIS. The use of a matrix of function, platform and communications media combinations to determine the overall scope of interoperability is innovative. Formal methods are outlined for specifying and measuring interoperability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Towards knowledge-based naval command systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Reports on various aspects of ARE's research on the application of KBS principles to problems in naval command and control. It outlines the problem domain, covering both operational and procurement issues, and outlines the rationale and the implications of introducing a new technical approach. It presents, as major components of naval C/sup 2/, the four topics of data fusion, tactical situation assessment, reactive resource allocation, and forward resource planning, and outlines activities in all four areas within ARE's programme of laboratory demonstrators. The advantages of combining these demonstrators within an integrated combat-management prototype are discussed, and the paper aims at implementing a subset of this overall concept as a major sea-going technology demonstrator.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evolving the user interface for knowledge-based command and control systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Describes work undertaken towards the provision of an effective interface between user and machine, including the increased opportunities and challenges offered by a knowledge-based solution. User evaluation of text, graphics and explanation facilities and formats, and the use of MMI design tools are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A general theory of command and control
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The paper sets out to produce a set of C/sup 2/ postulates, axioms and laws. The following proposed C/sup 2/ postulates and laws have been formulated: law of order/action rate equality, law of action/reporting rate equality, law of equipartition, law of infrastructure expansion, law of vertical data compression, law of decision rate invariance, law of lateral co-operation, law of survivability, postulate of decision scale invariance and postulate of command granularity. Additionally, equations have been produced which can be used to predict ideal values for: C/sup 2/ performance as a control mechanism, mean span of control, commander's direct communication links, commander's infrastructure links, mean hierarchy levels transversed per decision, mean hierarchy delay per decision, information content per C/sup 2/ information category, and communications capacity variation with information granularity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Reduced manning of a command system
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Describes a small scale study, funded by ARE, which looked at ways of reducing the number of men needed to operate and maintain the command system of a ship entering service at the turn of the century.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of modelling to assist C/sup 3/I system integration
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: System integration in the command control communication and intelligence (C/sup 3/I) domain involves the bringing together of a large number of separately procured, complex equipments to produce a system in which these constituent equipments are required to work harmoniously together. The approach to system integration which has been developed uses a combination of modelling techniques. Many of the techniques and disciplines associated with systems engineering have been widely applied on specific projects. However, a significant feature of the proposed approach is that systems engineering is undertaken not just for the individual equipments which comprise the system but also for the system as a whole. The approach also advocates that it is necessary to do not only logical (essential) modelling, but also dynamic (performance) modelling. The paper proceeds by describing the integration problem and then outlining various modelling techniques and tools. An overview of structured analysis is given and a number of dynamic modelling methods are discussed. Finally, the application of these techniques in system integration is reviewed with reference to a case study.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Security issues affecting C/sup 3/I systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Security issues and use of secure systems are currently being examined and scrutinised most closely, and are subject to some considerable visibility in the UK and NATO. Security issues have some major implications upon the design, implementation and operation of C/sup 3/I systems. The author describes some of the principal issues concerned with computer security of electronic systems-INFOSEC. The paper examines the impact of these issues upon design and acquisition of C/sup 3/I systems, formulation of policies, nature of threats and corresponding controls and the formal models of security policies/controls.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: BM/C/sup 3/ design by cumulative selection
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Introduces and explores the application of cumulative selection as a promising and exciting new way to approach the creation, design, development, management and operation of complex BM/C/sup 3/ systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The design and implementation of major upgrades to operational C/sup 3/I systems
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Second generation computer controlled C/sup 3/I systems have been in service for several years. Elements of these systems are now deployed in very significant numbers, and their performance makes a considerable contribution to the operational capability of the armed forces that they serve. At this stage in the maturity of these projects, significant enhancements and increases in operational capability need to be contemplated, designed and introduced into the system. To do this in a way that does not degrade the operational capability, either during the upgrade or after it, requires very careful thought and planning from the earliest stages of the project. The paper draws out the issues affecting the designer, the implementor, the maintainer and the operators of systems, and illustrates the techniques with the practical experience gained from upgrading the PTARMIGAN system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Toward a theory of combat with embedded command and control
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Reports the results of collaborative efforts aimed at developing models of combat with embedded command and control (C/sup 2/). The recent development of mathematical models of complex physical, chemical, biological, and ecological systems suggests that similar types of model can serve as a basis for models of military systems. The authors have developed combat models by using catastrophe theory, differential and difference equations, population- and systems-dynamics, chaotic dynamical systems theory, cellular automata, fractals, Q-analysis, Petri nets, and relativistic information theory, for example. Some of these models have been, or will be, implemented within a synthetic computer-based modelling environment called the electronic workbench. One of the most important discoveries made is that simple combat models can generate elaborate patterns of behavior and this has implications for the role that C/sup 2/ is playing, or should be playing, under such circumstances.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interoperability testing (military systems)
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The development of C/sup 2/I systems using an independent communications bearer system has made it necessary to consider how best to address interoperability testing. The paper reviews interoperability testing in the context of experience gained from the PTARMIGAN Tactical Communications System and the WAVELL Battlefield Command & Control System, both of which are now in service with the British Army.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A user interface design methodology and the implications for structured systems design methods
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: Summarises initial findings of an ongoing study directed toward the integration of human factors into Plessey's Systems Development Process Methodology. This study forms a part of the Plessey Joint Man-Machine Interface Programme, in which a number of Plessey businesses are collaborating on a range of activities relating to the design, evaluation and prototyping of user interfaces for a wide range of Plessey products.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design and specification of a warship combat system
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The paper has come about as the result of four years' intensive development work on a combat system, and it seems clear from this experience that the quality of personnel involved is no guarantee of a successful outcome. The problem seems to lie in a failure to keep pace with the technological nature of modern systems. This can be seen in three interconnected areas of difficulty: (a) it has led to a communications gap between the user and the engineer which makes it difficult for the former to explain his requirements in a form sufficiently informed and precise for the latter to implement; (b) it has tended to subordinate the system's essential purpose to the demands of the internal, often highly complicated, technology; (c) it has led to the possibility of systems with a size and level of sophistication well beyond the capacity of a single developer, or even a group of developers collaborating under existing methods. The author addresses these areas of difficulty by suggesting an approach which will ensure that the design and specification stages cease to be stumbling blocks in the development of a warship combat system. It advocates a disciplined system whereby the user's requirements are gathered, related to the environment with which the system must interact, and modelled in a way which is both faithful to the user's intentions and illuminating to the design team.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Domain modelling for requirements specification
publicationTitle: 1989 Third International Conference on Command, Control, Communications and Management Information Systems
abstract: The logical systems description project has been established to produce requirements specifications of future submarine command systems. The paper describes one particular aspect of this strategy, namely the development and use of reference models. It begins by outlining the LSD project strategy and goes on to describe why reference models are necessary. The development of explicit reference models takes place during domain analysis and is dealt with in some detail, describing the method used together with its application by the LSD project to produce five domain specific reference models. The use of these models by the project is illustrated, taking as an example the elicitation activity. Finally the LSD project experience is reviewed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
